name: Site percolation on the square lattice Z^2: a certified lower bound on p_c above van den Berg-Ermakov's 0.556 (1996) or an upper bound below Wierman-Oberly's 0.666894 (2024)
statement: In site percolation on the square lattice Z^2, each site is open independently with probability p. The threshold p_c^site(Z^2) is estimated as 0.59274605079210(2) (Jesper Jacobsen 2015, arXiv:1507.03027), but its rigorous bounds are far looser. Lower bounds: 0.503 (Toth 1985), 0.522 (Zuev 1988) and 0.541 (Mikhail Menshikov and K. D. Pelikh 1989). Then J. van den Berg and A. Ermakov reached 0.556 (Random Structures Algorithms 8 (1996) 199-212; CWI report R 9526). They modified Menshikov-Pelikh's growth-process comparison, using Strassen's coupling theorem and Fisher's inequality p_c(S) + p_c(S*) >= 1 for the matching lattice. Upper bounds: John C. Wierman's substitution method gave 0.679492 (Combin. Probab. Comput. 4 (1995) 181-188). John C. Wierman and Samuel P. Oberly lowered it to 0.666894 (Springer Proc. Math. Stat., 2024), the first improvement since 1995. A search on 2026-10-26 found no published improvement of either bound.
success_criterion: Success means either (a) a rigorous lower bound p_c^site(Z^2) >= p0 with p0 >= 0.5561, or (b) a rigorous upper bound p_c^site(Z^2) <= p0 with p0 <= 0.666794. Each must be at least 1e-4 better than the best published bound in that direction. That bound is the one found by a search of arXiv, Google Scholar and the works citing the 1996 paper and the 2024 chapter, re-run immediately before claiming. It is currently 0.556 for (a) and 0.666894 for (b). The claim is decided by a machine-checkable certificate with three parts. (i) A finite condition at p0, verified by a program in exact integer or rational arithmetic, or in outward-rounded interval arithmetic with an exact final comparison. (ii) The program that generates every number the condition uses from the stated definitions. A stranger must be able to rerun it from scratch, and a second implementation that shares no code must recompute the deciding margins. (iii) A written derivation that the finite condition implies the bound. It may use only published theorems cited by number, plus steps a skeptic can check line by line. Floating-point evidence and estimates do not count.
verification_method: Skeptic: (1) Rerun the exact checks at p0 with an independent implementation written from the definitions (seconds to hours). (2) As a calibration, use the same code to reproduce the published value of the method being extended: 0.556 for a van den Berg-Ermakov-type lower bound, or 0.679492 for a Wierman-type upper bound. (3) Read the derivation, especially the coupling step and the direction in which the matching-lattice inequality is used.
angles: Lower bound: van den Berg-Ermakov's growth process conditions on a finite window of the history. Larger windows, checked in exact arithmetic, give more.
Upper bound: Wierman's substitution method with larger substitution regions, as in Wierman-Oberly 2024.
pitfalls: Estimates (0.5927460508...) are not bounds. A 'lower bound' above it, or an 'upper bound' below it, indicates a bug.
Use the matching-lattice relation only in the direction that can be cited (Fisher's p_c(S) + p_c(S*) >= 1, as in the 1996 paper).
Checking marginals is not enough for Strassen's theorem: stochastic domination must hold for every increasing set.
Floating-point evidence is not a certificate.
